title: Why Novices shouldn't do Barbell Rows
summary: NH argues that bent-over barbell rows (and Pendlay rows) are misprogrammed: they are a hip-hinge/horizontal-pull hybrid that taxes the lower back, compete with squats and deadlifts, and get cheated with the legs, so novices should skip them. Novice programs include rows for their deadlift carryover, not for upper back growth. He recommends pull-ups for novices, then rows in a rotation with deadlifts or as strict upper-back work, with dumbbell rows as the best variation.
claims: There are no bad lifts, only bad applications; barbell rows are a poor lift for novices, and for most people, because they are done for the wrong reasons
Novice 'big five' programs (bench, squat, deadlift, overhead press, row) skip small muscles like wrists, calves and neck, claiming compounds cover them
The idea that compounds cover small muscles is false: novices end up two years in with big quads, glutes and chest and toothpick arms
None of his programs, novice or otherwise, include barbell rows
Rows won't build big biceps but they do grow the upper back
Programming rows at 3x5 or 5x5 is a mistake; treat the row as a muscular-endurance lift in higher reps and never grind the last rep
A properly done row can't keep gaining 10 lb a week for a year; people who manage that aren't really rowing
The barbell row is a hybrid of a hip hinge and a horizontal pull and taxes the posterior chain hard, but programs treat it as a pure horizontal pull
Rows after squats or deadlifts on the same day are bad programming because of the stacked lower back demand
A row means holding a deadlift position, stabilizing with hamstrings, glutes and lower back, and pulling; novices who can't deadlift properly can't do that safely
Novices should not barbell row, and most intermediates should stay away from it too
Most people row with a deadlift-like torso angle because a truly horizontal position is too taxing, which shows they shouldn't be rowing
A real Pendlay row: torso fully horizontal, no lower-body help, uncontrolled negative; anything else is just a row
Deadlifts and rows in the same program compete: either the deadlift progresses and the row stalls, or the novice sandbags the deadlift
Never program heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day; a heavy squat plus a low-intensity hinge variation is fine
Most people row with their arms and legs and barely recruit the upper back, yet see strength gains
About a year earlier he rowed 315 lb for sets of 15 with a cheating, RDL-like style driven mostly by his legs
Test your row on an incline bench with the same torso angle and legs off the floor; your weight will drop far below your standing row
Cheat rows don't isolate the upper back, just as cheat curls don't isolate the biceps
Rows fill novice programs because of their carryover to the deadlift, being in the same line of specificity, not for upper back growth
Size and strength feed each other but are different qualities; moving more weight doesn't automatically mean more growth
Many novices get stronger on rows simply because they are bulking and getting fatter
Prioritize pull-ups over rows for novices; they build the back and keep bodyweight in check relative to strength
A natural calisthenics athlete has a wider, more defined back than a natural powerlifter because he trains the back directly
Use rows in rotation with deadlifts, e.g. deadlift on Monday and row instead of deadlifting on Friday
Kroc-style cheat rows carry over well to the deadlift but cause trouble if done after deadlifting
Option: one heavy deadlift top set to failure, then 1-2 easy row warm-ups and 2-3 heavy row back-off sets; never heavy rows followed by deadlift back-offs
Once past the novice stage with a solid deadlift, strict braced rows can be an upper back builder; superset them with bench or put Pendlay rows on arm day
Avoid supinated Yates rows because of biceps tendon risk; do them braced against a rack with minimal cheat
Rows shine for mid-back thickness; pull-ups are unbeatable for the lats
Dumbbell rows are the best row variation: no lower back tax, and the arc path lets the lat fully stretch
His novice program uses cable rows (dumbbell rows are a valid swap) so novices learn to use the lower back on deadlifts before it has to bridge a row

hip-hinge hybrid that taxes the lower back; not for novices
fully horizontal, no lower body, let negative drop
exposes how much leg drive standing rows use
preferred over rows for novices; best for lats

pull in an arc outside the body to stretch the lat
